topStories.headline: Mission Mourns Dolores Huerta: Balmy Alley Vigil Honors Labor Icon at 96
topStories.dek: The co-founder of the United Farm Workers died on October 28, and dozens gathered that same evening in the Mission's mural-lined Balmy Alley to remember her.
topStories.body:
Dolores Huerta, the legendary labor organizer and civil rights leader who co-founded the United Farm Workers alongside César Chávez, died on October 28, 2026, at the age of 96. Her passing reverberated with particular force in San Francisco's Mission District, where she had deep roots and where her spirit is woven into the neighborhood's murals, political history, and activist culture.

Within hours of her death, several dozen people gathered for a candlelight vigil in Balmy Alley — the narrow, mural-lined block between 24th and 25th streets that has long served as the Mission's open-air gallery of Chicano political art. Friends and longtime colleagues shared memories and lit candles beneath an altar assembled in her honor.

At the vigil, Joshua Arce, a longtime local political figure who knew Huerta personally, recalled her ceaseless drive to organize. Mission Local reported that Arce described how Huerta had spent hours at his Balmy Alley home just last year, working the phones to persuade California state assembly members to support a congressional redistricting ballot measure. For Huerta, political work was never finished.

Muralists in Balmy Alley also spoke of Huerta's influence on the Mission's Chicano arts movement. The group Mujeres Muralistas, which has painted murals in the Mission since the 1970s, counted Huerta as an inspiration — someone who showed women they could take front-line roles in movements that had historically sidelined them, according to the SF Standard.

Huerta's ties to San Francisco's Mission District spanned decades. She was a frequent presence at rallies and organizing drives in the neighborhood, and her image appears in several Mission murals. The street-renaming ordinance passed by the Board of Supervisors just last week — changing Cesar Chavez Street to Las Campesinas — carries fresh resonance now, honoring the farmworker women Huerta championed throughout her life.

topStories.headline: Real Estate Pours $2.7 Million Into Fight Against SF Social Housing Measure Before Tuesday Vote
topStories.dek: Proposition I would lock roughly $120 million a year in luxury-property transfer taxes into affordable and social housing — and the development industry has mounted the most expensive campaign against any measure on the November 3 ballot.
topStories.body:
San Francisco voters go to the polls on November 3, and one of the most bitterly contested measures on the ballot has deep roots in Mission District housing politics: Proposition I, the Affordable Housing Guarantee Act. The measure would dedicate half of the city's transfer tax revenue from property sales over $10 million to affordable housing, social housing developments, homelessness prevention, and rental assistance — with no new taxes imposed.

Opponents — a coalition of developers, real estate investors, and major property owners — have raised more than $2.7 million to defeat the measure, according to Mission Local, making it the largest opposition war chest against any November ballot measure in the city. Prominent donors include billionaire venture capitalist Michael Moritz, who gave $200,000 to the no campaign. National firms Related California and Kilroy Realty are also listed among the funders. Mayor Daniel Lurie has come out against Prop I, arguing it strips the General Fund of roughly $120 million a year in discretionary revenue the city would otherwise control.

Proponents say the city has been sidestepping the will of voters since 2020, when residents approved both a higher transfer tax on luxury property sales and an ordinance allowing the city to develop up to 10,000 units of low-income rental housing — commitments that were never fully acted upon. The San Franciscans for Social Housing coalition gathered more than 20,000 signatures to place the measure on the November ballot, submitting them to City Hall on July 2, 2026. Supporters argue the redirected revenue could fund European-style mixed-income social housing — a model common in cities like Vienna — rarely attempted in the United States.

Opponents counter that a separate measure on the same ballot, Proposition C, already boosts the city's Housing Trust Fund to $125 million a year without the same restrictions on General Fund spending. The dueling measures have opened a sharp divide among affordable-housing advocates heading into election week.

topStories.headline: Mission District Parking Lot Will Finally Become Apartments — After Five Years of Delays
topStories.dek: A 152-unit, nine-story building at 321 Florida Street is set to break ground in November, backed by a $61.7 million construction loan and poised to become only the second large market-rate apartment project to start construction in San Francisco since 2023.
topStories.body:
A half-acre surface parking lot on Florida Street between 16th and 17th streets in the Mission District has sat empty for years while a housing project worked through city approvals, financing struggles, and community negotiations. That wait is nearly over: developer DM Development and investment firm Ascentris announced in September that construction at 321 Florida Street is expected to begin in November 2026, backed by a $61.7 million construction loan from PNC Bank in their first joint venture together.

The project was city-approved in 2021 but never broke ground. Its 152 units will include studios, one-bedrooms, and two-bedrooms; 15 of those units are designated affordable, serving households ranging from very low-income to moderate-income. The nine-story building was designed by local firm Handel Architects, and completion is anticipated in late 2028. Residents will be close to Franklin Square, Potrero Center, and the 16th Street BART station.

The launch matters beyond the block: according to the developers' press release, 321 Florida will be only the second market-rate apartment building with more than 28 units to break ground in San Francisco since 2023, a sign that financing conditions may be shifting after years of near-total construction paralysis in the city.

The project also carries some contested history. Before the 2021 approval, the developer had made community commitments — including a $2 million contribution toward an affordable housing site at 2675 Folsom Street and a dedicated nonprofit gallery space — that subsequently lapsed without being fulfilled. Those agreements are no longer binding. A 1,500-square-foot ground-floor space is now planned as an event venue for Cultura y Arte Nativa de las Americas, an educational nonprofit focused on Latin American, Caribbean, African, and Indigenous cultures.

events.title: Cine+Más SF Latino Film Festival — Closing Weekend
events.description: The 18th annual Cine+Más San Francisco Latino Film Festival wraps up its run with final screenings this weekend. The festival has brought films from across the U.S., Latin America, and Spain to venues throughout the city since October 22.

events.title: Día de los Muertos: Festival of Altars at Potrero del Sol Park
events.location: Potrero del Sol Park (La Raza Park), 2827 Cesar Chavez St., Mission District
events.description: The Marigold Project hosts its 34th annual Festival of Altars, free and open to all ages. This year's theme is "Familia: Entre raíces y el Cielo" (Family: Between Roots and Heaven). Community altar-building begins at 10 a.m., a sunset blessing ceremony follows at 5 p.m., and live performances by La Gente SF and Mariachi San Carlos begin at 7 p.m.

events.title: Día de los Muertos: 45th Annual Procession in the Mission
events.description: Organized by the Comité de Rescate Cultural, the 45th annual Día de los Muertos Procession steps off at 7 p.m. from 22nd and Bryant streets, traveling through the neighborhood to honor loved ones who have passed. Aztec dancers and danzantes gather at 6 p.m. The event is free.

events.title: Mission Branch Library Grand Reopening Celebration
events.location: Mission Branch Library, 3359 24th Street (at Bartlett), Mission District
events.description: After more than six years of closure and a $36.5 million renovation, the historic Carnegie-funded Mission Branch Library reopens with a free community celebration. The Valencia Street temporary branch closes permanently on October 31; the newly renovated building includes dedicated spaces for teens and children.

moreNews.headline: Fire Displaces Eight From Bernal Heights Building Near Alemany Farmers Market
moreNews.body: A one-alarm fire broke out before dawn on Wednesday, October 28, in a commercial building on the 900 block of Peralta Avenue in Bernal Heights, not far from the Alemany Farmers Market. San Francisco Fire Department crews battled the blaze for roughly one hour before containing it at approximately 5:41 a.m. No injuries were reported. Eight occupants were displaced, and the American Red Cross responded to assist. The cause of the fire had not been released as of press time.

moreNews.headline: Valencia Street Briefly Closed After Suspicious Package Found at Mission Police Station
moreNews.body: A suspicious package outside the Mission District Police Station prompted police to close Valencia Street between 17th and 18th streets on the evening of Thursday, October 29. Officers spotted the package at approximately 8:10 p.m. and the Department of Emergency Management alerted nearby residents to avoid the area. The package was determined to be safe and the street was fully reopened.
